retrieved.label: E3 @ 11:04
retrieved.text: You don't see the molecule directly, you see its diffraction shadow, and from the geometry of that shadow you can work backward to the shape that cast it. The people doing this for DNA, and doing it superbly, were at King's College in London, Morris Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin. And this is the photo 51 I've heard about. This is photo 51. Rosalind Franklin produced an X-ray diffraction image of DNA, the sharpest anyone had taken, and to a trained eye it screams two things. First, the overall pattern is a big, bold X-shape of smeared spots, and that X is the unmistakable signature of a helix. A helix, a spiral, diffracts X-rays into exactly that cross pattern. It's a dead giveaway. Second, the spacings between the marks encode the dimensions, how wide the helix is and how far you go along it before the spiral repeats.

retrieved.episode_title: Great Papers 03 The Double Helix, Watson and Crick 1953
retrieved.label: E3 @ 39:00
retrieved.text: Photo 51 was her image taken in her lab. Her measurements of the diameter and the repeat were among the hardest, most decisive numbers. And a crucial fact about how the story actually went, that photograph and a report containing her unpublished measurements were shown to Watson without her knowledge or agreement. So the data that let the model click into place was hers, and it reached Cambridge through a side door. And she didn't share in the recognition the way the others did. She did not. The Nobel Prize for this work was awarded in 1962 to Watson, Crick and Wilkins. Rosalind Franklin had died in 1958 of cancer at 37 and the prize is not given after death, so she could not have shared it in 1962 regardless. But that technicality shouldn't be allowed to smooth over the fuller point. During her life her contribution was underweighted, both in the moment and in the popular telling for decades afterward, and the use of her data without her consent is a real part of how the discovery was made.

retrieved.episode_title: Great Papers 03 The Double Helix, Watson and Crick 1953
retrieved.label: E3 @ 0:55
retrieved.text: It's the answer to the deepest question in biology, precisely because it's a shape, and that's the thing I most want you to feel by the end of the hour, that here, uniquely, the structure of the molecule and the mechanism of life turn out to be the same discovery. So here's our plan. First I'll set up the problem they were actually facing, which is stranger than, what does DNA look like? It's, what kind of object could possibly do the two jobs a gene has to do at once? Then we'll lay out the clues on the table in 1953, because they didn't work in the dark. There were three big hints, and one of them is a photograph. Then we'll build the structure, piece by piece, the way they built it. Two chains, a backbone, and the pairing rule that is the whole ballgame. And then we'll cash out that understated sentence, how a shape tells you how life copies itself, and deal squarely with the story of who got the credit.

retrieved.episode_title: Great Papers 03 The Double Helix, Watson and Crick 1953
retrieved.label: E3 @ 38:07
retrieved.text: So the chain is complete, base sequence, read in triplets, spells an amino acid sequence, which folds into a protein, and it all rests on there being a stable, copyable sequence in the first place, which is what the double helix delivered. Before we get to legacy, we have to talk about the credit, because you promised to deal with it squarely, and it's a real part of this story. Rosalind Franklin, where does she sit in what we just described? She sits much closer to the centre than the famous two-name paper makes it look, and I'll lay it out plainly, without turning it into either a fairy tale or a courtroom. The X-ray evidence that the molecule is a helix of specific dimensions, clue 3, the one that constrained the whole model, came in large part from Rosalind Franklin's work. Photo 51 was her image taken in her lab. Her measurements of the diameter and the repeat were among the hardest, most decisive numbers.

retrieved.episode_title: Great Papers 04 Shannon and the Birth of Information, 1948
retrieved.label: E4 @ 32:08
retrieved.text: Every scratched CD or DVD that still plays perfectly is error correction quietly repairing the damage, exactly as the coding theorem promised. Every photograph beamed back across billions of miles from a probe out past Pluto, arriving faint and buried in noise, gets through because it was encoded against a channel whose capacity Shannon taught us to compute. Hard drives, Wi-Fi, the entire Internet, moving unimaginable rivers of bits with near-perfect fidelity, all of it operates in the space Shannon defined, using the framework he built. Who was Shannon, though? Was information theory his one big idea, or one of several? Remarkably, it wasn't even his first foundational one. About a decade earlier, still a young man, his master's thesis showed that electrical switching circuits, networks of simple relays and switches, could carry out logic, true and false, and or, not, the operations of Boolean algebra.

retrieved.episode_title: Great Papers 04 Shannon and the Birth of Information, 1948
retrieved.label: E4 @ 6:50
retrieved.text: One bit is the amount of information in a single yes or no answer, when the two possibilities were equally likely beforehand. It's the resolution of one perfectly balanced either or. The cleanest way to feel it is the game of twenty questions. I'm thinking of something, you ask yes or no questions to pin it down. Each good question, one where yes and no are equally likely, cuts the remaining possibilities in half. And each such halving is exactly one bit of information. If there are two possibilities and I tell you which, that's one bit. Four possibilities and you need two bits. Two good questions to nail it down. Eight possibilities, three bits. Every time you double the number of possibilities, you need one more bit to specify the answer. So a bit is a halving. And the word itself, bit, where does that come from? It's a contraction of binary digit, a digit that's one of two values, which we usually write as a zero or a one.
